title: Multi-Link Operation (MLO)
summary: One connection that holds links in several bands, and moves traffic between them without reconnecting.

opener.promise: One connection with links in several bands
opener.problem: Badge calls break up when the one band a device uses gets busy.

beats.heading: The call that breaks up between units

caption.headline: The call that breaks up between units
caption.takeaway: Choppy badge calls cost clinical time and create repeat pages: a care problem, not just IT.

beats.body:
A nurse takes a call on a [[voice-badge]] while walking to the next unit. The badge is connected to the nearest [[access-point]] on a single band — and on that band, an imaging cart has just started a large upload.

The call's small voice packets now wait in line behind the image. The nurse hears gaps and repeats themselves, or the call drops.
beats.bottomLine: Choppy or dropped badge calls cost clinical time and create repeat pages — a reliability problem for care teams, not just an IT inconvenience.
beats.sceneDescription: An access point on the left connects to a nurse's badge on the right with a single arched link. Large gray blocks from an imaging upload fill the link, and the badge's small voice packets bunch up behind them and stall.

beats.heading: One connection, several radio lanes

caption.headline: One connection, several radio lanes
caption.takeaway: Links in 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz{{mlo-bands}}; in [[str|STR]], the badge sends and receives at once{{str-what}}.

beats.body:
[[mlo|Multi-Link Operation]] lets a device and an access point form one connection with links in more than one band {{mlo-defined-be}}: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz {{mlo-bands}}.

Here the badge uses its 5 GHz and 6 GHz links in **[[str|STR]]** mode: it sends its side of the call on 6 GHz while it receives the other side on 5 GHz, at the same time {{str-what}}. When one band gets busy, traffic can move to another link without the device reconnecting first {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. Whether a device can use a pair of bands this way depends on its hardware.
beats.bottomLine: Urgent traffic gets another lane on a different band, instead of waiting for one busy band to clear.
beats.sceneDescription: One access point on the left connects to the nurse's badge on the right with three arched links, one each in 6 GHz, 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz. In STR mode the badge sends its voice on the 6 GHz link while it receives voice on the 5 GHz link, at the same time; the 2.4 GHz link stays connected and ready.

questions.q: Is MLO just bonding bands together for speed?
questions.a: Speed is one use, but the bigger gain for clinical traffic is resilience: a device keeps links in several bands{{mlo-bands}}, so urgent packets can move to a free band without reconnecting.

beats.heading: Watch the call change bands

caption.headline: The call switches bands mid-call
caption.takeaway: When an upload fills 5 GHz, incoming voice moves to 6 GHz without reconnecting{{mlo-tid-mapping}}.

beats.body:
The call starts split across two links: the badge sends on 6 GHz and receives on 5 GHz. Then the imaging cart's upload arrives on the 5 GHz band, and the incoming voice packets begin to wait behind it.

Because the badge already holds the 6 GHz link in the same connection, the incoming voice moves there and keeps flowing, with no reconnecting first {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. Now 6 GHz carries both sides of the call, and the 2.4 GHz link stays ready as another option.
beats.bottomLine: The call keeps going on another band while the busy band clears, instead of waiting in line behind the upload.
beats.sceneDescription: The badge sends its voice on the 6 GHz link and receives voice on the 5 GHz link. Gray imaging-upload blocks then fill the 5 GHz link and the incoming voice packets briefly wait. The incoming voice moves to the 6 GHz link, which now carries the call in both directions, while the 2.4 GHz link stands ready.

beats.heading: New in Wi-Fi 7: no reconnecting

caption.headline: Earlier Wi-Fi: one lane at a time
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 6 and 6E use one band at a time{{single-link-pre-be}}; Wi-Fi 7 keeps the others open.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 6E devices connect on one band at a time. If that band gets busy, the device can only wait, or reconnect on another band and briefly pause its traffic {{single-link-pre-be}}. With Wi-Fi 7, the other links are already set up, so traffic moves without reconnecting {{mlo-tid-mapping}}.

For care teams, that means steadier voice calls and alerts while clinicians move. How much a device gains depends on how it uses its links, so check each badge, phone and laptop model.
beats.bottomLine: Plan MLO with device refresh: the access points enable it, but each clinical device model decides how much it gains.
beats.sceneDescription: The view splits in two. On the left, an earlier-generation connection uses a single link that clogs with upload traffic while voice packets wait. On the right, the Wi-Fi 7 connection has three links open, and the voice packets move to the free one and keep flowing.

questions.q: Does MLO replace roaming between access points?
questions.a: No. MLO links one device to one access point across its bands{{mlo-defined-be}}. Moving between access points is still roaming, so roaming design still matters.
Password-based sign-in over Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections requires WPA3{{wpa3-mlo-required}}, so plan the WPA3 migration together with the MLO rollout.

questions.q: Will our current badges and phones get MLO?
questions.a: Only if they support Wi-Fi 7 multi-link operation, which needs new hardware. Ask each vendor how the model uses its links; that decides how much it gains.

cisco.text: On a Cisco network that mixes WPA2 and WPA3 sign-in, devices that join with WPA2 cannot use multi-link operation or Wi-Fi 7{{cisco-wpa2-no-mlo}}.
